{{Short description|Class of quartic plane curves}}
[[File:Cassini-3kurv.svg|300px|thumb|Three Cassini ovals, differing by the range within which the parameter {{mvar|e}} (equal to {{math|''b''/''a''}}) falls:
{{legend-line|green solid 2px|{{math|0 < ''e'' < 1}}}}
{{legend-line|red solid 2px|{{math|''e'' {{=}} 1}}}}
{{legend-line|blue solid 2px|{{math|1 < ''e'' < {{sqrt|2}}}}}}
Not shown: {{math|''e''  ≥ {{sqrt|2}}}} (convex).]]

In [[geometry]], a '''Cassini [[oval]]''' is a [[quartic plane curve]] defined as the [[locus (mathematics)|locus]] of points in the [[plane (geometry)|plane]] such that the [[Product (mathematics)|product]] of the distances to two fixed points ([[Focus (geometry)|foci]]) is constant. This may be contrasted with an [[ellipse]], for which the ''sum'' of the distances is constant, rather than the product. Cassini ovals are the special case of [[polynomial lemniscate]]s when the [[polynomial]] used has [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] 2.

Cassini ovals are named after the astronomer [[Giovanni Domenico Cassini]] who studied them in the late 17th century.<ref>Cassini</ref> 
Cassini believed that a planet [[orbit]]ing around another body traveled on one of these ovals, with the body it orbited around at one focus of the oval.{{sfn|Cohen|1962}}
Other names include '''Cassinian ovals''', '''Cassinian curves''' and '''ovals of Cassini'''.

==Formal definition==
[[File:Cassini-k-def0.svg|300px|thumb|Cassini oval: <math>|PP_1| \!\!\;\times\!\!\; |PP_2| = b^2</math> for any location of ''P'' on the curve]]
A '''Cassini oval''' is a set of points, such that for any point <math>P</math> of the set, the ''product'' of the distances <math>|PP_1|,\, |PP_2|</math> to two fixed points <math>P_1, P_2</math> is a constant, usually written as <math>b^2</math> where <math>b > 0</math>: 
:<math>\{P : |PP_1| \!\!\;\times\!\!\; |PP_2| = b^2 \}\ .</math>
As with an ellipse, the fixed points <math>P_1,P_2</math> are called the ''foci'' of the Cassini oval.

==Equations==
If the foci are (''a'',&nbsp;0) and (−''a'',&nbsp;0), then the equation of the curve is
:<math>((x-a)^2+y^2)((x+a)^2+y^2) = b^4.</math>
When expanded this becomes
:<math>(x^2+y^2)^2-2a^2(x^2-y^2)+a^4 = b^4.</math>

The equivalent [[polar coordinates|polar]] equation is
:<math>r^4-2a^2r^2 \cos 2\theta = b^4-a^4.\,</math>

==Shape==
[[Image:Line of Cassini.svg|300px|thumb|right|Some Cassini ovals. (''b''&nbsp;=&nbsp;<span style="color:#a00;">0.6''a''</span>, <span style="color:#808;">0.8''a''</span>, <span style="color:#00a;">''a''</span>, <span style="color:#088;">1.2''a''</span>, <span style="color:#0a0;">1.4''a''</span>, <span style="color:#880;">1.6''a''</span>)]]

The curve depends, up to similarity, on {{math|1=''e'' = ''b''/''a''}}. When {{math|''e'' < 1}}, the curve consists of two disconnected loops, each of which contains a focus. When {{math|1=''e'' = 1}}, the curve is the [[lemniscate of Bernoulli]] having the shape of a sideways figure eight with a [[double point]] (specifically, a [[crunode]]) at the origin.<ref>Basset p. 163</ref><ref>Lawden</ref> When {{math|''e'' > 1}}, the curve is a single, connected loop enclosing both foci. It is peanut-shaped for <math>1 < e < \sqrt{2}</math> and convex for <math>e \geq \sqrt{2} \,.</math><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php/Cassini_oval |title = Cassini oval - Encyclopedia of Mathematics}}</ref> The limiting case of {{math|''a'' → 0}} (hence {{math|''e'' → &infin;}}), in which case the foci coincide with each other, is a [[circle]].

The curve always has ''x''-intercepts at {{math|±&thinsp;''c''}} where {{math|1=''c''<sup>2</sup> = ''a''<sup>2</sup> + ''b''<sup>2</sup>}}. When {{math|''e'' < 1}} there are two additional [[real number|real]] ''x''-intercepts and when {{math|''e'' > 1}} there are two real ''y''-intercepts, all other ''x''- and ''y''-intercepts being imaginary.<ref>Basset p. 163</ref>

The curve has double points at the [[circular points at infinity]], in other words the curve is [[circular algebraic curve|bicircular]]. These points are biflecnodes, meaning that the curve has two distinct tangents at these points and each branch of the curve has a point of inflection there. From this information and [[Plücker formula|Plücker's formulas]] it is possible to deduce the Plücker numbers for the case {{math|''e'' ≠ 1}}: degree =&nbsp;4, class =&nbsp;8, number of nodes =&nbsp;2, number of cusps =&nbsp;0, number of double tangents =&nbsp;8, number of points of inflection =&nbsp;12, genus =&nbsp;1.<ref>Basset p. 163</ref>

The tangents at the circular points are given by {{math|1=''x'' ± ''iy'' = ±&thinsp;''a''}} which have real points of intersection at {{math|(±&thinsp;''a'', 0)}}. So the foci are, in fact, foci in the sense defined by Plücker.<ref>See Basset p. 47</ref> The circular points are points of inflection so these are triple foci. When {{math|''e'' ≠ 1}} the curve has class eight, which implies that there should be a total of eight real foci. Six of these have been accounted for in the two triple foci and the remaining two are at 
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \left(\pm a \sqrt{1-e^4}, 0\right) &\quad (e<1), \\
  \left(0, \pm a \sqrt{e^4-1}\right) &\quad (e>1).
\end{align}</math>
So the additional foci are on the ''x''-axis when the curve has two loops and on the ''y''-axis when the curve has a single loop.<ref>Basset p. 164</ref>

== Cassini ovals and orthogonal trajectories ==
[[File:Cassini-hyp.svg|300px|thumb|Cassini ovals and their orthogonal trajectories (hyperbolas)]]
''[[Orthogonal trajectories]]'' of a given [[Pencil (mathematics)|pencil]] of curves are curves which intersect all given curves orthogonally. For example, the orthogonal trajectories of a pencil of [[Confocal conic sections|confocal]] ellipses are the confocal [[hyperbola]]s with the same foci. For Cassini ovals one has:
*The orthogonal trajectories of the Cassini curves with foci <math>P_1, P_2</math> are the [[equilateral hyperbola]]s containing <math>P_1, P_2</math> with the same center as the Cassini ovals (see picture).

'''Proof:'''<br>
For simplicity one chooses <math>P_1 = (1,0),\, P_2 = (-1,0)</math>. 
:The Cassini ovals have the equation <math display="block">f(x,y) = (x^2+y^2)^2 - 2(x^2-y^2) + 1 - b^4 = 0.</math>
:The [[equilateral hyperbola]]s (their [[asymptote]]s are rectangular) containing <math>(1, 0), (-1, 0)</math> with center <math>(0, 0)</math> can be described by the equation <math display="block">x^2 - y^2 - \lambda x y - 1 = 0,\ \ \ \lambda \in \R.</math>
These conic sections have no points with the ''y''-axis in common and intersect the ''x''-axis at <math>(\pm 1, 0)</math>. Their [[conic section#General Cartesian form|discriminants]] show that these curves are hyperbolas. A more detailed investigation reveals that the hyperbolas are rectangular. In order to get normals, which are independent from parameter <math>\lambda</math> the following implicit representation is more convenient 
<math display="block">g(x,y) = \frac{x^2 - y^2 -1}{xy} - \lambda  = \frac{x}{y} - \frac{y}{x} - \frac{1}{xy} - \lambda = 0 \; .</math>
A simple calculation shows that <math>\operatorname{grad}f(x,y) \cdot \operatorname{grad}g(x,y) = 0</math> for all <math>(x,y),\, x \ne 0 \ne y</math>. Hence the Cassini ovals and the hyperbolas intersect orthogonally.

''Remark:''<br>
The image depicting the Cassini ovals and the hyperbolas looks like the [[Equipotential curve|equipotential]] curves of two equal [[point charge]]s together with the lines of the generated [[electrical field]]. But for the potential of two equal point charges one has <math>1/|PP_1| + 1/|PP_2| = \text{constant}</math>. (See [[Implicit curve]].) Instead these curves actually correspond to the (plane sections of) equipotential sets of two infinite wires with equal constant line [[charge density]], or alternatively, to the level sets of the sums of the [[Green’s function]]s for the Laplacian in two dimensions centered at the foci.

The single-loop and double loop Cassini curves can be represented as the orthogonal trajectories of each other when each family is coaxal but not confocal. If the single-loops are described by <math>(x^2+y^2)-1=axy</math> then the foci are variable on the axis <math>y=x</math> if <math>a>0</math>, <math>y=-x</math> if <math>a<0</math>; if the double-loops are described by <math>(x^2+y^2)+1=b(x^2-y^2)</math> then the axes are, respectively, <math>y=0</math> and <math>x=0</math>. Each curve, up to similarity, appears twice in the image, which now resembles the field lines and potential curves for four equal point charges, located at <math>(\pm1,0)</math> and <math>(0,\pm1)</math>. Further, the portion of this image in the [[upper half-plane]] depicts the following situation:  The double-loops are a reduced set of congruence classes for the central Steiner conics in the hyperbolic plane produced by direct collineations;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sarli |first=John |date=April 2012 |title=Conics in the hyperbolic plane intrinsic to the collineation group |journal=Journal of Geometry |volume=103 |issue=1 |pages=131–148 |doi=10.1007/s00022-012-0115-5 }}</ref> and each single-loop is the locus of points <math>P</math> such that the angle <math>OPQ</math> is constant, where <math>O=(0,1)</math> and <math>Q</math> is the foot of the perpendicular through <math>P</math> on the line described by <math>x^2+y^2=1</math>.

==Examples==
The second [[commons:Image:Lemniscates5.png|lemniscate of the Mandelbrot set]] is a Cassini oval defined by the equation <math>L_2=\{c: \operatorname{abs}(c^2 + c)=ER \}.</math>  Its foci are at the points ''c'' on the [[complex plane]] that have orbits where every second value of ''z'' is equal to zero, which are the values 0 and −1.

== Cassini ovals on tori ==
[[File:Tor-cass-1-3.svg|400px|thumb|Cassini ovals as planar sections of a torus (the torus on the right is a [[spindle torus]])]]
Cassini ovals appear as planar sections of [[torus|tori]], but only when the cutting plane is parallel to the axis of the torus and its distance to the axis equals the radius of the generating circle (see picture).

The intersection of the torus with equation
:<math>\left(x^2+y^2+z^2 + R^2 - r^2\right)^2 = 4R^2 \!\left(x^2+y^2\right)</math>
and the plane <math>y=r</math> yields
:<math>\left(x^2+z^2 + R^2\right)^2 = 4R^2 \!\left(x^2+r^2\right).</math>
After partially resolving the first bracket one gets the equation
:<math>\left(x^2+z^2\right)^2 -2R^2(x^2-z^2)= 4R^2r^2-R^4,</math>
which is the equation of a Cassini oval with parameters <math>b^2 = 2Rr</math> and <math>a = R</math>.

== Generalizations ==
Cassini's method is easy to generalize to curves and surfaces with an arbitrarily many defining points:
*<math>|PP_1| \times |PP_2| \times \cdots \times |PP_n| = b^n</math>
describes in the planar case an [[implicit curve]] and in 3-space an [[implicit surface]].
